'''''Spiraea alba''''', commonly known as '''meadowsweet''',<ref name="GRIN">{{GRIN |access-date=10 June 2014}}</ref> '''white meadowsweet''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SPAL2|taxon=Spiraea alba|access-date=27 November 2015}}</ref> '''narrowleaf meadowsweet''',<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Spiraea alba (Meadowsweet, Narrowleaf Meadowsweet, White Meadowsweet) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/spiraea-alba/ |access-date=2025-11-22 |website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref> the botanical '''pale bridewort''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> or '''pipestem''',<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Yarnell |first=Richard Asa |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DSfgDwAAQBAJ&dq=Spiraea+alba+pipe&pg=PA180 |title=Aboriginal Relationships between Culture and Plant Life in the Upper Great Lakes Region |date=1964 |publisher=University of Michigan Press |isbn=978-1-949098-22-8 |page=180 |language=en}}</ref> is native to the wet soils of the [[Allegheny Mountains]] and other portions of eastern [[North America]],<ref>{{cite book |author=Venable, N.J. |author2=Service, W.V.U.C.E. |year=1996  |title=Common Summer Wildflowers of West Virginia |publisher=West Virginia University Extension Service}}</ref> but is currently endangered in the state of Missouri{{Citation needed|reason=Not listed as endangered by any regulatory body, including Missouri Department of Conservation as of January 2024: https://mdc.mo.gov/sites/default/files/2024-03/SOCC%20Checklist%202024_ADA_0.pdf|date=November 2025}}. It is [[naturalized]] in other parts of the world.<ref name=GRIN/>

==Description==
Narrowleaf meadowsweet shrubs typically mature to 3-4 feet in height with a similar spread.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Meadowsweet |url=https://www.canr.msu.edu/nativeplants/meadowsweet |access-date=2025-11-22 |website=Native Plants and Ecosystem Services, MSU |language=en-us}}</ref> This species is often the most conspicuous part of the vegetation in its habitat, taking up large areas of ground. Its leaves are glossy yellow-green, oblong or lance-shaped, and toothed on the edges, and its twigs are tough and yellowish brown. Fall foliage is golden yellow.<ref name=":1" /> The white and sometimes pink fragrant flowers grow in spike-like clusters at the ends of the branches, blooming from early summer through September. The brown fruit, which persists after flowering, is a distinctive feature of all ''Spiraea'' species.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://newfs.s3.amazonaws.com/taxon-images-1000s1000/Rosaceae/spiraea-alba-latifolia-fr-ahaines.jpg |format=JPG|title=Photographic image|website=Newfs.s3.amazonaws.com|access-date=28 March 2022}}</ref>

==Ecology==
Butterflies<ref>{{Cite web |title=Spiraea alba - Plant Finder |url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=286372 |access-date=2024-11-23 |website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org}}</ref> and other beneficial insects like bees<ref name=":2" /> visit the plant for nectar and pollen. In autumn brown seed capsules appear and are fed on by songbirds. Glossy green foliage turns yellow in the fall. Deer tend to leave this plant alone. Meadowsweet is a host plant for the larvae of the [[Celastrina argiolus|spring azure butterfly]] (''Celastrina argiolus'').<ref name=":1" />

==Uses==
The blooms make a good cut flower.

The hollow, upright stems were used historically as pipe stems.<ref name=":0" />
